python.001.title: A Computer Follows Instructions
python.001.mental_model: A program is a precise, ordered list of instructions. The computer does exactly what you say, in the order you say it.
python.001.why_this_matters: Every program is instructions. Understanding this removes fear.
python.001.engineering_context: Production code executes these instructions millions of times. Precision matters.

python.002.title: Program vs Result
python.002.mental_model: Same input + different instructions = different output. Code is the recipe; result is the dish.
python.002.why_this_matters: Beginners think code does something magically. The instruction→result chain is foundational.
python.002.engineering_context: Two functions with same name but different logic produce different results. The code IS the difference.

python.003.title: Input → Process → Output
python.003.mental_model: Every program takes input, transforms it, and produces output. That's the IPO cycle.
python.003.why_this_matters: This is the universal structure of all software. From calculators to social media feeds.
python.003.engineering_context: A web API takes a request (input), processes it (database lookup, business logic), and returns a response (output).

python.006.title: A Named Box
python.006.mental_model: A variable is a named box that holds a value. The name stays, the contents can change.
python.006.why_this_matters: Every program you'll ever build starts with storing data in variables. Without variables, programs can't remember anything between lines.
python.006.engineering_context: Variables hold user inputs, API responses, database records, and UI state. A todo app's items are variables. A game's score is a variable.

python.007.title: Assignment Is Updating
python.007.mental_model: Assignment copies the current value. It doesn't create a link. Changing the source later doesn't change the destination.
python.007.why_this_matters: This misconception cascades into every later topic. If you think assignment links variables, you'll never understand state.
python.007.engineering_context: In a shopping cart, setting total = price doesn't link them. Changing price later doesn't change total. That's why we recompute.
python.007.builds_toward: State management, immutability, React hooks, database updates

infosys_infytq.intuition_hint: InfyTQ has output prediction with reassignment

hook.question: You set a = 5, then b = a, then change a to 10. What is b now?

steps.scene: Arrow copies value from A to B
Box B still shows 5 — no link!

interact.prompt: After a = 5; b = a; a = 10; what is b?

predict.prompt: If x = 3 and y = x, then x = 7, what is y?
predict.explanation: Assignment copies the value at that moment. No link is created.

build.solution:
price = 100
discount = price
price = 50
print(discount)  # Still 100!

break.buggy_code:
a = 5
b = a
a = 10
print(b)  # Expects 10, gets 5
break.expected_failure: b is 5, not 10 — the link doesn't exist
break.question: Why doesn't b change when a changes?

fix_steps: To keep them in sync, you must assign again
debug.answer: Copy is one-time. Reassign to update.

retrieve.prompt: After b = a, changing a later...

python.008.title: Assignment Can Use the Old Value
python.008.mental_model: The right side is evaluated FIRST using the old value, THEN the result is written back. score = score + 5 means: read old score, add 5, write new score.
python.008.why_this_matters: This is the single most important assignment pattern. Every loop counter, every accumulator, every state update uses it.
python.008.engineering_context: request_count = request_count + 1 is the foundation of analytics, counters, and every incremental update in production systems.

tcs_nqt.intuition_hint: TCS NQT asks about self-referential assignment

steps.scene: Arrow writes 15 back into the same cell

interact.prompt: Change the initial score and see what happens:

predict.prompt: If score = 3 and then score = score + 4, what is score?
predict.explanation: Right side uses the OLD value (3 + 4 = 7), then writes 7.

break.buggy_code:
score = 10
score = score + 5
score = score + 5
print(score)
break.expected_failure: Output is 20, not 15 — each line updates the current value
break.question: Why is the final score 20, not 15?

fix_steps: Third line uses the NEW score (15) + 5 = 20
debug.answer: Each update uses the latest value

retrieve.answer: read the old value, add 1, write the new value

python.009.title: Multiple Variables
python.009.mental_model: State is everything the program remembers right now. More variables = richer state. Each variable is independent.
python.009.why_this_matters: Real programs track many facts simultaneously. A user has a name, age, email, and login status — all in different variables.
python.009.engineering_context: A user object in a database has many fields. Each field is like a variable. Changing 'email' doesn't change 'name'.
python.009.builds_toward: Objects, dictionaries, database records, API payloads

python.010.title: State Detective
python.010.mental_model: A program's state is the current values of all variables. Predicting state changes is a core debugging skill.
python.010.why_this_matters: Every bug is a state mismatch. If you can't trace state, you can't debug.
python.010.engineering_context: Production debugging often means: 'What was the value of X when Y happened?' State tracing is that skill.

tcs_nqt.intuition_hint: TCS NQT has state tracing puzzles

hook.question: Three statements modify memory. Can you predict the final state before running?

steps.scene: x = 5, y = 3 appear on a state board

interact.prompt:
Predict the final state:
a = 4
b = a + 1
a = 10

predict.prompt: After x=5, y=x, x=2, what are x and y?
predict.explanation: y = x copies the value at that moment. Later changes to x don't affect y.

build.starter_code:
# Trace the state
a = 3
b = a + 2
a = 7
# What are a and b now?
print('a =', a)
print('b = b)
build.solution:
